rv.q: The show is sheer, nerve-shredding escapism - I jumped out of my skin several times.
Cheryl emerges from the ectoplasm with more than the ghost of a chance of taking her stage career further.
It’s a minor shame because the play still compels, entertains and unnerves.
Without getting too carried away, it’s Cheryl – whoo-hoo – who has opened a portal to another world of possibility.
Suffice to say Olivia Colman and Jodie Comer won’t be feeling threatened but if Cheryl intends to launch an acting career then this is not a bad start.
For its faults, I can’t deny the enjoyment I got out of 2:22, which is far funnier than it is scary.
It's still a very entertaining evening, however, with Robins' text and Matthew Dunster's staging laced with hints, red herrings and Gothic tropes.
But as Dunster’s production has churned through its various casts, it has started to feel sloppier, more faded, a ghost of its original.
But it would be pushing it to say it was a classic play, and its longevity increasingly feels like a triumph of casting over anything else.
The production ultimately succeeds not because of its ramped up comedy but in spite of it.
It is just a shame that this really doesn’t live up to its hype.
2:22 A Ghost Story is gripping throughout, exploring themes of class, relationships, science and religion.

cn.t: Cheryl makes a respectable West End debut in this gripping supernatural thriller that continues to prove itself a crowd-pleasing phenomenon, even if critics find it more psychologically astute than genuinely terrifying.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Lyric Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.

sg.vl: Good sound, check the seat map
sg.ra: Lyric Theatre's own seating notes flag possible obstructed views from the rear orchestra — sound still carries well, but check the seat map before booking here.
At 1,930 seats, Lyric Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's largest houses (1,930 seats across four levels), the Lyric's sheer scale means rear orchestra and mezzanine seats sit far from the stage, with sightline obstructions from balcony overhangs. Acoustics are solid and the theater's modern construction makes it well-suited for spectacle productions.

acc.note: 42nd St entrance at street level with elevator to Orchestra and Dress Circle. No elevator to Balcony.
